chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
title: Sidney Bechet and Benny Carter as giants
summary: He heard Bechet with Noble Sissle's band, with Eddie Cole on bass, and praises Benny Carter's cultured style.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend

blocks.x: You've got some interesting looking notes there. What are they?

No, I just -- I wanted to mention Sidney Bechet who was one of the great saxophonists, you know, and a lot of the musicians aren't aware of how great he was. He was with Noble Sissle's band, and I used to go to see them

quite often. And here was a man that was a giant. Also in that same band, playing bass, was Eddie Cole, Nat's brother, who also played piano. You're aware of Eddie Cole. But he was a bass player with that band. Noble Sissel had just returned from Europe, and this was the first time I'd really got a chance to see Bechet in person and here was a giant who had contributed so much. You know, he had such a unique style, and he played soprano saxophone which was just beautiful, you know.
And then there was -- what can I say, but like Benny Carter. These -- here was another giant whose style was altogether different. A very cultured style, you know, very schooled, warm.
And also he was a master of quite a few instruments.
Quite a few instruments. Trumpet, yes, piano.
Yeah, yeah. But these -- I think the kids should check up on -- go back and see what these guys have contributed and listen to what they did. Because as I say Bechet was a true giant.
He was, I think, one of the four musicians that Duke always cited as being the most important.
Musicians in jazz history, (2nd) one of his principal influences.
